1.note: Here Jeremiah is speaking as if the descendants of Jacob were a **house**, that is, a single family living together. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [people of the nation of Israel]

2.note: Jeremiah is using the phrase **Thus says Yahweh** to introduce a direct quotation of what Yahweh told him to say. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language.

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the customs and practices of the nations were a **way**, that is, a road that a person could travel along. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Do not learn the practices of the nations]

This is a double negative, consisting of the negative particle **not** and the negative word **dismayed**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [remain calm]

The implication is that **the signs of the heavens** are events such as eclipses and the movements of the stars, which the people of the nations regarded as omens that predicted the future. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and do not be dismayed at events in the sky that people think foretell the future]

The word translated as **for** indicates how this statement relates to the command that comes before it. This could mean: (1) that it gives the reason why the people of Israel should not be dismayed, since fearing these signs is what the nations do or (2) that it concedes that the nations are indeed dismayed by these signs, even though the people of Israel should not be. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [because it is the nations who are dismayed by them]

3.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if the customs of the peoples were **breath**, that is, something that has no substance and quickly disappears. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the customs of the peoples have no substance and soon vanish]

The pronoun **he** refers to the **craftsman** who is named later in this verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [for a woodworker cuts down a tree from the forest]

The implication is that the man cuts down the tree in order to carve an idol out of the wood. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [for a man cuts down a tree from the forest to make an idol]

Here, **hands** represents the skill and the labor of the craftsman who shapes the wood. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the skilled work of a craftsman]

4.q: בְּ⁠כֶ֥סֶף וּ⁠בְ⁠זָהָ֖ב יְיַפֵּ֑⁠הוּ בְּ⁠מַסְמְר֧וֹת וּ⁠בְ⁠מַקָּב֛וֹת יְחַזְּק֖וּ⁠ם
4.note: The pronoun **he** refers to the craftsman who carves the idol, and the pronoun **they** refers to the workers who help him. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [With silver and gold the craftsman decorates it; with nails and hammers his workers fasten it]

This is a double negative, consisting of the negative particle **not** and the negative word **totter**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [so that it will stand firm]

5.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **scarecrows of a cucumber field** are lifeless figures that cannot do anything, so idols are lifeless objects that cannot do anything. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [as lifeless as scarecrows standing in a cucumber field]

The term **scarecrows** describes figures that people set up in their fields to frighten away birds that would eat the crops. If your readers would not be familiar with what scarecrows are, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [like lifeless figures that people set up in a cucumber field]

Yahweh is repeating forms of the verb **carrying** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [people always have to carry them]

The expression **they are carried** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [people carry them]

Yahweh is using the expression **there is not good with them** as a common expression of the culture to mean “they are not able to do anything good.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and also they are not able to do anything good]

This is a double negative, consisting of the negative particle **not** and the negative word **afraid**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [Be confident about them]

This is a double negative, consisting of the negative particle **not** and the negative word **harm**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [they are harmless]

6.note: Here, **your name** represents Yahweh himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and you yourself are great in power]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **power**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and your name is great because you are mighty]

7.note: Jeremiah is using the question form to affirm that everyone should fear Yahweh, the **king of the nations**. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Everyone should certainly fear you, king of the nations!]

Jeremiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [For fearing you is what you deserve]

Jeremiah is using the adjective **wise** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase, and use the masculine form if your language marks that distinction. Alternate translation: [among all the wise people of the nations]

8.note: The pronoun **they** refers to the people of the nations who make and worship idols. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And in one those idol worshipers are stupid and foolish]

Jeremiah is using the expression **in one** as a common expression of the culture to mean “one and all.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And without exception]

The terms **stupid** and **foolish** mean similar things. Jeremiah is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [they are utterly senseless]

Here, **wood** represents the wooden idols that people carve. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [their worthless instruction comes from a wooden idol]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **instruction**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what worthless idols teach]

9.note: The expression **is brought** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use those forms, you could express the ideas in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Merchants bring silver that workers have beaten from Tarshish]

Jeremiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and gold is brought from Uphaz]
The word **Uphaz** is the name of a place.

10.q: מִ⁠קִּצְפּ⁠וֹ֙ תִּרְעַ֣שׁ הָ⁠אָ֔רֶץ וְ⁠לֹֽא־יָכִ֥לוּ גוֹיִ֖ם זַעְמֽ⁠וֹ
10.note: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **anger** and **indignation**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [The earth quakes because he is angry, and the nations cannot endure it when he becomes furious]

Here, **his indignation** represents the punishment that Yahweh sends when he is indignant. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the punishment he sends when he is indignant]

11.note: The pronoun **them** refers to the people of the nations who worship idols. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [to the idol-worshiping nations]

Jeremiah is referring to all of creation by naming two major components, **the heavens** and **earth**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [everything that exists]

12.q: עֹשֵׂ֥ה אֶ֨רֶץ֙ בְּ⁠כֹח֔⁠וֹ מֵכִ֥ין תֵּבֵ֖ל בְּ⁠חָכְמָת֑⁠וֹ
12.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [I am talking about the one who, by his very great power and wisdom, made the entire earth]

Jeremiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is the maker of the earth]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **power**, **wisdom**, and **understanding**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [by being strong, the establisher of the world by being wise, and by understanding everything]

Here Jeremiah is speaking as if the **heavens** were a large piece of cloth that Yahweh spread out above the earth. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he created the expanse of the heavens above the earth]

13.note: The implication is that **a tumult of waters in the heavens** is the noise of a rainstorm that Yahweh sends. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [there is a roar of stormy rain that he sends in the sky]

Jeremiah is using the expression **from the end of the earth** as a common expression of the culture to mean “from the far horizon.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the far horizon] or [from far away]

Here Jeremiah is speaking as if Yahweh kept the wind in **storehouses**, that is, buildings where valuable things are kept until they are needed. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he sends out the wind that he has kept ready]

14.note: Jeremiah says **Every man** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [Many men are stupid]

Here the masculine term **man** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [Every person is stupid]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **knowledge**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and knows nothing]

A **cast image** is an idol that a craftsman makes by pouring melted metal into a mold. If your readers would not be familiar with what a cast image is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [his metal idol]

Here Jeremiah is speaking as if the idols that people cast from metal were **a lie** itself, when it actually represents the lie that it can help those who worship it. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for his cast image lies to people]
Here, **breath** represents life. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and there is no life in them]

15.note: The pronoun **They** refers to the carved images and cast images that Jeremiah speaks about in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Those idols are vapor]

Here Jeremiah is speaking as if idols were **vapor**, something that has no substance or value. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [insubstantial and worthless]

Jeremiah is using **a work of mockeries** as a common expression of the culture to mean “something that people should ridicule.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [something deserving of ridicule]

Jeremiah is using the expression **at the time of their visitation** as a common expression of the culture to mean “when Yahweh punishes them.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when Yahweh comes to punish them]

16.note: Here Jeremiah is comparing Yahweh to the **portion** that the descendants of Jacob received, that is, the share of land that a family was allotted as its own. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The God who has been allotted to the descendants of Jacob is not like these idols]

Here, **Jacob** represents the people who were descended from Jacob. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Jacob’s descendants]
The pronoun **he** refers to Yahweh, not to Jacob. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is the one who formed all things]

Here Jeremiah is speaking as if the people of Israel were an **inheritance**, that is, property that a person receives permanently from his family. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and Israel is the tribe that belongs permanently to him]

17.note: Even though Jeremiah is speaking to a group of people, **you** and **your** are singular in this verse. If the singular forms of these pronouns would not be natural in your language, you could use the plural forms in your translation.

The implication is that the people are to pack up their belongings because their enemies will soon take them away from their land. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Pack up your belongings from the land, ready to be carried into exile]

The implication is that **you one who dwells in the siege** refers to the people of Jerusalem, whose city an enemy army has surrounded. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [you people of Jerusalem, whose city an enemy army has surrounded]

18.note: Yahweh is using **Behold me** as an expression that people of this culture would commonly use to mean that he was about to do something. He does not mean that people should look at him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Now I am about to sling]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if he were **slinging** the people who live in the land, that is, hurling them far away as a person hurls a stone from a sling. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Behold, I am about to hurl far away the ones who inhabit the land]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [so that they are found out] or [so that they will experience the punishment]

19.note: The pronoun **me** refers to the one who is lamenting this disaster. This could mean: (1) Jeremiah, who grieves over what is happening to his people. Alternate translation: [Woe to me, Jeremiah, because of my breaking] or (2) the city of Jerusalem, which speaks as if it were a person. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Woe to Jerusalem, the city of God, because of her breaking]

Jeremiah is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of grief and distress. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [How terrible it is for me]

Here Jeremiah is speaking as if the disaster that has come upon his people were a **breaking**, that is, a bone that has been fractured. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [because of the ruin that has come upon me]

Here Jeremiah is speaking as if the calamity that has come upon his people were a **wound** on his own body. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [My suffering is severe]
Jeremiah is using the phrase **But I said** to introduce a direct quotation of his own words. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language.

20.note: The expressions **is devastated** and **are ripped apart** are passive verbal forms. If it would be unnatural to use those forms, you could express the ideas in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Invaders have devastated my tent, and they have torn apart all of my cords]

Here Jeremiah is speaking as if the ruin of his people were a **tent** that has collapsed because its cords have been torn apart. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [My people are ruined, like a tent that has collapsed with all of its cords ripped apart]

Jeremiah is referring to the loss of his sons in a polite way by using the phrase **they are not**. Depending on what is helpful for your readers, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [and they are dead]

21.note: The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because]

Here Jeremiah is speaking as if the leaders of the people were **shepherds**, men who guide and care for flocks of sheep. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the leaders of the people]

Here Jeremiah is speaking as if worshiping Yahweh and asking him for guidance were to **seek** him, as a person searches for something that is lost. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they do not worship Yahweh or ask him for guidance]

The expression **is scattered** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and their enemies have scattered all their flock]

Here Jeremiah is speaking as if the people whom the leaders guide were a **flock** of sheep. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and all the people they lead are scattered]

22.note: Jeremiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Listen to the sound of a report]

Jeremiah is using the term **Behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Now listen]

The implication is that **a great commotion from the land of the north** is the noise that an invading army makes as it marches toward Judah. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and a great commotion made by an invading army from the land of the north]

Here, **a dwelling place of jackals** represents a place that is deserted and ruined, since jackals live where people no longer live. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [a place where no one lives anymore]

The term **jackals** describes wild animals that resemble dogs and that live in deserted places. If your readers would not be familiar with what jackals are, you could use the name of a similar animal that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [wild dogs]

23.q: כִּ֛י לֹ֥א לָ⁠אָדָ֖ם דַּרְכּ֑⁠וֹ לֹֽא־לְ⁠אִ֣ישׁ הֹלֵ֔ךְ וְ⁠הָכִ֖ין אֶֽת־צַעֲדֽ⁠וֹ
23.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about **his way** before the information about **a man**. Alternate translation: [that his way does not belong to a man, and that walking and making firm his steps is not for a man]

Here Jeremiah is speaking as if the course of a person’s life were **his way**, that is, a road that he travels along. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that a person does not decide how his life will go]

Jeremiah is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [of any person]

Here Jeremiah is speaking as if living from day to day and deciding what will happen were **walking** and taking **steps** along a road. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [living his life and determining what will happen to him]

24.note: The word translated as **Discipline** is an imperative, but it communicates a request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a request. Alternate translation: [Please discipline me, Yahweh]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **justice** and **anger**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [but justly, not when you are angry]

Jeremiah is using the word translated as **lest** to introduce an outcome that he does not want to happen. Because of this, he first gives Yahweh an instruction to follow so that this will not happen. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that avoiding this outcome is the purpose of the instruction. Alternate translation: [otherwise]

The implication is that if Yahweh were to **diminish** Jeremiah and his people in his anger, he would reduce them to nothing and destroy them completely. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [so that you do not reduce me to nothing]

25.q: שְׁפֹ֣ךְ חֲמָתְ⁠ךָ֗ עַל־הַ⁠גּוֹיִם֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר לֹֽא־יְדָע֔וּ⁠ךָ וְ⁠עַל֙ מִשְׁפָּח֔וֹת אֲשֶׁ֥ר בְּ⁠שִׁמְ⁠ךָ֖ לֹ֣א קָרָ֑אוּ
25.note: The word translated as **Pour out** is an imperative, but it communicates a request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a request. Alternate translation: [Please pour out your fury on the nations that do not know you and on the clans that do not call on your name]

Here Jeremiah is speaking as if Yahweh’s **fury** were a liquid that could be poured out on the nations. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Send your furious punishment]
Here, **your name** represents Yahweh himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [on you]

Here Jeremiah is speaking as if the enemies of his people had **consumed** them as an animal devours the prey that it catches. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they have destroyed Jacob]

Jeremiah is repeating forms of the verb **consumed** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [for they have completely consumed Jacob]

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [and they have completely destroyed him]

Here, **Jacob** represents the people of Israel, who are descended from Jacob. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the people of Israel]
